title: Describing functions and the small-gain idea

sections.heading: The idea

sections.body_md:
Gain and phase are linear words. A relay, a saturation, or a dead zone does not have one gain. The describing function keeps the one number that matters for a nearly sinusoidal oscillation: the gain of the fundamental, as a function of amplitude. Higher harmonics are left out on purpose.

Plotted as \(-1/N(a)\), that gain becomes a locus a linear Nyquist curve can intersect. An intersection is a candidate limit cycle: a frequency from the plant curve and an amplitude from the nonlinearity. The small-gain idea is the linear cousin of the same picture. If the product of two gains stays below 1, the perturbation cannot push the loop through the critical point.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
An ideal relay of levels \(\pm M\), driven by \(a\sin\omega t\), has
\[
N(a) = \frac{4M}{\pi a}.
\]
It is real, positive, and falls as \(a\) grows. A unit-slope saturation that clips at \(\pm M\) keeps \(N = 1\) for \(a \le M\). For larger \(a\), with \(\delta = M/a\),
\[
N(a) = \frac{2}{\pi}\left(\sin^{-1}\delta + \delta\sqrt{1-\delta^2}\right).
\]
Balance against a linear plant \(G\) is \(G(j\omega) = -1/N(a)\). The small-gain bound says that a peak gain \(1.8\) tolerates an uncertain gain only up to its reciprocal.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A relay with levels \(\pm 6\) sees a sine of amplitude 2. The describing function is \(4\cdot 6/(\pi\cdot 2) = 12/\pi \approx 3.82\). The matching critical point is \(-1/N \approx -0.262\), on the negative real axis. If the plant Nyquist curve crosses the real axis at \(-0.262\), this amplitude is the predicted oscillation. A plant that never gets closer to the origin than \(0.1\) on the negative real axis does not intersect \(-1/N\) for this relay, so the approximation predicts no cycle.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: \(N(a)\) is a gain, so the locus is \(-1/N\), not \(-N\). An odd memoryless map has a real describing function; hysteresis is what adds phase. The third harmonic of a relay is a third of the fundamental, which is small only if the plant kills it. If the plant amplifies that harmonic, the sine-in, fundamental-out story is wrong and the predicted amplitude can be badly off. Small-gain is sufficient, not necessary: a larger perturbation can still be stable if its phase does not point at the critical point.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Robust stability turns the small-gain idea into a test on \(T\) and a multiplicative weight. Lyapunov arguments cover the same nonlinear loop without dropping harmonics. Adaptive schemes change the linear gain on purpose, which moves the Nyquist curve relative to \(-1/N(a)\) and can create or destroy the intersection.
